analysis.one_liner: Repeals the ban on exporting American crude oil and other energy export restrictions.
analysis.headline: The bill to lift the ban on exporting American crude oil was introduced in December 2014 and died in committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the decades-old ban on exporting crude oil produced in the United States, and barred any federal official from imposing such a restriction in the future. It also would have repealed existing export limits on coal, natural gas, and petroleum products, and ordered a study of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the government's emergency oil stockpile. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to committees and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic oil producers, who could sell US crude to overseas buyers at higher world prices rather than selling to domestic refineries. The Energy Department would also gain a mandate to review the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that no federal official may impose or enforce any restriction on exporting crude oil, allowing domestic producers to sell crude to foreign buyers at world prices.

It also repeals existing authority to restrict exports of coal, petroleum products, natural gas, and petrochemical feedstocks, and directs the Energy Department to study whether the Strategic Petroleum Reserve is the right size and composition.

analysis.who_pays: American consumers, who could face higher gasoline and heating fuel prices if domestic crude is shipped to foreign markets instead of US refineries.

drawbacks.text: Removing the export ban would allow domestically produced crude to be sold to foreign buyers, which could push up prices American consumers pay for gasoline and other refined products.
The bill would also repeal existing export controls on coal, natural gas, and petroleum products, going beyond crude oil and expanding exports of fossil fuels more broadly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If enacted, consumers could face higher gasoline and heating oil prices as domestic crude flows overseas, while oil producers gain access to world prices; the SPR study would be a genuine but modest safeguard. The bill never got far enough for the trade-off to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2014, referred to House committees and a subcommittee, and never advanced before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 9, 2014, in the final weeks of the 113th Congress.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Foreign Affairs committees and then to the Energy and Power Subcommittee on December 12, 2014, with no further action.
The bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, without any vote in the House or Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: American consumers, who kept the existing protections that keep domestic crude available to US refiners; the oil export ban remained in place until a separate law repealed it later that year.

for.name: Rep. Joe Barton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the crude oil export ban.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, but the bill never got far enough for a partisan vote to occur.

industries.note: The bill would let producers sell domestically pumped crude oil to foreign buyers at world prices instead of limiting sales to US refineries, lifting a 1970s-era restriction.
Refiners have profited from access to cheaper domestic crude under the export ban; allowing exports could raise their input costs while opening new markets for refined products.

industries.industry: American consumers of gasoline and heating fuel
industries.note: With more domestic crude shipped overseas, US fuel prices could rise, though the size of the effect was debated.
